What muscle groups are used in archery? I was thinking the same thing but I do a lot of strength training with weightlifting.

In recurve the draw and hold should be in your back (watch an Olympian like Ki Bo Bae shoot and watch her draw arm shoot backward when she releases the string due to the tension in her back). Lats to keep the bow steady and your shoulder level (and in the case of Olympic archery you use your lats to position your sight rather than your arm), traps and rhomboid for drawing back and expanding, a bit of triceps for your bow arm (the one you hold the bow in), and delts for raising the bow. Other important muscles are abdominals, which should be active to support the back and keep posture during the shooting sequence, glutes, which are flexed during the shooting sequence, and any leg work that will help you keep completely grounded and sturdy if you are a target archer.

Most people I've seen who look buff haven't put nearly as much work on their back as they have on their arms and mistakenly try to draw and hold with their arms rather than their back. Really, no new archer should pull back more than 20lbs or so anyway even if they could because it will make it more difficult to learn proper form. It's better to start off with a low poundage and focus on good form than shoot with a high poundage and struggle with form.

The way compound bows work is you aren't holding the full draw-weight at full draw, there's what's call the wall where the weight lets off. You'll see that compound archers actually hold at full draw for much longer than traditional archers do, the cam wheels allow for this let off, giving the archer more time to sight down either the arrow or use their sight pins. You can also sometimes see where the let off is when watching archers, or videos of them. Traditional bows only allow for a second or two of sighting because you are holding the full draw-weight with those bows.

The constant raising and lowering of the bow-arm can also keep it strong and help balance it out. Even at just 8 pounds, after 40-50 targets and 4-some odd miles of hiking, it's just as tired as my arrow-arm. Your arrow-arm is also almost always your dominant arm, anyway.

I push back against my bow a little as I pull back on the string. You're supposed to pull your shoulder blades together as you draw, as if holding a walnut there, rather than give all the strength to one arm or the other. It strangely evens itself out, I've never noticed more strength in one side over the other, other than the standard "right side is stronger" because I'm right handed, if that makes sense.
